newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says "major crisis" in Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says "major crisis" in Mideast peace.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Wednesday the Middle East peace process was in a "major crisis" and urged all concerned parties to rescue it.
He was speaking to reporters after Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat discussed ways to revive talks between Palestinians and Israel.
The talks have been on hold since Israel started building on March 18 a new 6,500-home Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in 1967 and later annexed.
On March 21, a Palestinian militant opposed to peace killed himself and three Israelis in a Tel Aviv cafe bombing.
Moussa said Arafat briefed Mubarak on "the situation in the occupied territories and the peace process and how to deal with the current crisis".

Moussa said he and Arafat would meet further "to find out how to save the peace process and return it to its natural path. We have a major crisis on our hands now and all of us have to cooperate to put an end to it or emerge from it.

"We are trying to find the best way to revive the peace process, which can never be revived alongside the policy of settlements and particularly things that affect Jerusalem and its status," Moussa added.
Israel claims all of Jerusalem as its undivided capital while Palestinians want the eastern part to be the capital of their future state.
Palestinians see Jewish settlement-building as pre-empting "final status" peace talks which have yet to resume since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took power last June.

Arafat did not speak to reporters after meeting Mubarak but said in an interview published in an Israeli daily on Wednesday the Middle East was headed for "the abyss" if Netanyahu's policies were not blocked.
Mubarak said in a German newspaper interview this week that a six-month suspension of settlement-building could restart the peace process.
"The idea is a moratorium on the building of settlements in order to pave the way for meaningful negotiations," Moussa said.
"It is very difficult to assume or to think that negotiations would continue in a constructive atmosphere while bulldozers are working to settle the territories."
Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel and has often mediated in peace talks between the Jewish state and its Arab neighbours.
But Cairo has become increasingly critical of Israeli policies since the right-wing Netanyahu came to power.
